latest_findings.description: ShimCache (AppCompatCache) confirms subject_srv.exe execution: CacheEntryPosition=434, Path=C:\windows\subject_srv.exe, LastModifiedTimeUTC=2018-04-10 19:29:48, Executed=Yes. This is the 4th independent source corroborating T1070.006 timestomping — ShimCache faithfully recorded the backdated 2018-04-10 $SI LastModified timestamp that the attacker planted, proving the backdating survived into the AppCompatCache. Cache positions 0-35 are Chrome 88 auto-update installers (modified Jan 2021), placed at lower positions because Chrome auto-update ran AFTER the attack, meaning the system rebooted post-Sep-16 and flushed the in-memory cache to disk. Subject_srv.exe at position 434 confirms it was added to the cache during the attack window and was not re-executed after Chrome's last update run.
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis: ShimCache Executed=Yes flag could be set by a compatibility check that did not involve actual execution; the 2018-04-10 timestamp could reflect a legitimately old binary that predates the investigation.
evidence_against_it: MFT confirms subject_srv.exe was CREATED on 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC (EntryNumber 29211) — a 2018 binary cannot predate its own MFT creation record.
Prefetch SUBJECT_SRV.EXE-*.pf records 2 executions on 2021-09-16 at 02:52:10 and 03:01:58 UTC, confirming the Executed=Yes flag corresponds to real process execution.
USN Journal records BasicInfoChange|Close at 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC on subject_srv.exe confirming the $SI timestamp was modified at close — the 2018 date is the result of attacker timestomping.

latest_findings.description: Mnemosyne.sys is ABSENT from ShimCache (488 total entries checked). This is expected for two compounding reasons: (1) Windows AppCompatCache does not typically track kernel driver (.sys) files — only PE executables loaded in user mode; (2) Mnemosyne.sys was dropped to C:\Windows and deleted within a ~10-minute window (USN: FileCreate 02:52:10, FileDelete 03:01:03, FileCreate 03:01:59 on 2021-09-16) — too short for shimming to occur. Absence from ShimCache is consistent with the attacker's BYOVD ephemeral driver pattern (T1014/T1068) and does not contradict the USN/EVTX/Registry evidence of driver deployment.
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis: Mnemosyne.sys might have been expected in ShimCache if AppCompatCache tracked kernel drivers, providing another persistence corroboration point.
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis_not_applicable_re: Absence of Mnemosyne.sys from ShimCache is fully explained by (1) AppCompatCache not tracking .sys files and (2) its ephemeral on-disk window — this is a structural limitation, not an evidentiary gap. No conclusion about Mnemosyne's use can be drawn from this absence.

latest_findings.description: Seven independent artifact sources confirm F-Response Subject Agent (subject_srv.exe) was deployed by an attacker from BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) to acquire the full disk image of base-wkstn-01 via raw kernel-level access, exfiltrating approximately 1.55 GB at 2021-09-16 03:07 UTC — constituting unauthorized full-disk exfiltration (T1005 + T1041) enabled by the F-Response BYOVD kernel driver (Mnemosyne.sys, T1014/T1068).
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis: subject_srv.exe is an authorized forensic imaging tool operated by the victim organization's own IT or security team conducting a legitimate disk acquisition of the workstation.
evidence_against_it: EVTX EID 4624 shows the authentication to base-wkstn-01 came from BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) using shieldbase\cbarton-a credentials via NTLM LogonType 3 — a lateral network logon, not a locally initiated authorized imaging session.

subject_srv.exe was timestomped to 2018-04-10 (USN BasicInfoChange|Close at 03:01:57 UTC confirms intentional $SI backdating) — authorized forensic tools are never timestomped as this would violate chain of custody.

Mnemosyne.sys kernel driver was installed and deleted within a 10-minute window (USN: drop at 02:52:10, delete at 03:01:03, reinstall at 03:01:59) — covert ephemeral driver pattern; authorized acquisitions maintain driver artifacts for the case record.
DKOM: conhost.exe PID 214668 was hidden from pslist via kernel linked-list unlinking (rootkit T1014) — legitimate forensic tools do not conceal companion processes.

latest_findings.description: Four independent artifact sources confirm the attacker timestomped subject_srv.exe to 2018-04-10 19:29:48 UTC at time of deployment (2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC) to evade timeline analysis and blend with legitimate binaries (T1070.006): MFT $SI<$FN divergence with uSecZeros=True and Copied=True flags, USN Journal BasicInfoChange|Close record at true creation time, ShimCache recording the backdated 2018-04-10 LastModifiedTimeUTC, and Registry AppCompatCache also preserving the backdated value.
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis: The 2018-04-10 timestamp reflects the legitimate compilation/packaging date of subject_srv.exe — an older binary version of F-Response that was installed from an archive without modification.
evidence_against_it: MFT $FN (the NTFS-kernel-maintained timestamp, not modifiable by user-mode APIs) shows EntryNumber 29211 was created on 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC — a 2018-compiled binary cannot have an MFT $FN creation time in 2021.

MFT uSecZeros=True flag: the microsecond fields of all four $SI timestamps are exactly zero — a statistical impossibility for a genuine file modification and the signature of timestomping tools that zero the sub-second component.

USN Journal (authoritative change log written by the NTFS kernel, cannot be forged) records an 0x800 (BasicInfoChange) reason code at close of the 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC write sequence — proving the $SI timestamps were changed at the moment the file was written, not pre-existing.
latest_findings.fk_confidence_note: FK multiplier 0.80 applied for mft_timestomp. Original: 0.980 -> Adjusted: 0.784

latest_findings.description: Three independent sources confirm attacker-controlled host BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) laterally accessed base-wkstn-01 using compromised domain credential shieldbase\cbarton-a via NTLM network logon, then immediately deployed F-Response as a service to perform the disk acquisition (T1550.002 / T1021.002): EVTX EID 4624 NTLM LogonType 3 burst from 172.16.5.25 at 02:51:50 UTC, memory network connection subject_srv.exe established to 172.16.5.25:5682 (F-Response controller port), and EID 7045 service install of 'F-Response Subject' at 03:01:57 UTC within 10 minutes of the logon burst.
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis: BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) is a legitimate IT administration workstation and the cbarton-a logon represents authorized remote administration of the workstation.
evidence_against_it: F-Response Subject Agent (a commercial disk acquisition tool) was installed as a Windows service immediately following the logon — authorized IT administration does not deploy raw disk imaging tools on workstations without documented change control.
Mnemosyne.sys (F-Response kernel driver) was loaded ephemerally and deleted within 10 minutes — covert operational security behavior incompatible with authorized administration.
DKOM rootkit technique was active during the session (conhost.exe PID 214668 hidden from pslist) — rootkit activity is not consistent with authorized IT work.
The logon used NTLM (not Kerberos) — NTLM is used when the attacker authenticates with a captured hash (Pass-the-Hash) or when the source machine is not domain-joined.

latest_findings.description: VSS analysis of /evidence/disk/base-wkstn-01-c-drive.E01: found 3 shadow copies. Shadow copy dates: Aug 27, 2021 13:52:18.153389500 UTC to Sep 14, 2021 23:53:09.062631700 UTC.

VSS enumeration found 3 Volume Shadow Copies on the C: drive — all pre-dating the 2021-09-16 attack: VSS1 (2021-08-27 13:52:18 UTC, 20 days before), VSS2 (2021-09-05 19:53:10 UTC, 11 days before), VSS3 (2021-09-14 23:53:09 UTC, 2 days before — matches Amcache coverage boundary). Shadow copy directories were not accessible via vshadowmount at analysis time (SIFT tool limitation), preventing artifact recovery. Critically: no EID 1102 (Security log cleared) was detected in sigma_hunt, and no vssadmin delete shadows command is evidenced — the attacker did NOT delete shadow copies. VSS3 (Sep 14) pre-dates the attack by 2 days and may contain pre-attack registry hives (SYSTEM, SECURITY, SAM) and EVTX covering the Feb 2021 Mnemosyne prior-install window if the log was not yet overwritten.
latest_findings.alternative_hypothesis: Shadow copies were deleted by the attacker using vssadmin or WMI and the vshadowinfo output is showing stale/phantom metadata.
evidence_against_it: sigma_hunt on Security.evtx (E-021) found no EID 4688 process creation for vssadmin.exe or wmic.exe with delete shadows arguments.
All 3 shadow copies have valid GUIDs and attribute flags 0x0042000d (standard Windows VSS flags) reported by vshadowinfo — deleted shadow copies would not appear in vshadowinfo output at all.
The shadow copy creation timestamps are plausible automatic Windows backup schedule dates (weekly/bi-weekly spacing), consistent with legitimate automatic VSS creation.

unresolved_discrepancies.description: Registry confirms F-Response persistence: (1) HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Services — 'F-Response Subject' service entry written at 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC (matches EID 7045 and USN Journal precisely); (2) 'mnemosyne' service has TWO entries — one with Name last write 2021-09-16 03:01:59 (attack day reinstall) AND a second with Name last write 2021-02-03 21:51:45 — indicating the Mnemosyne kernel driver was PREVIOUSLY installed approximately 7 months before the attack (T1543.003). The 2021-02-03 date coincides with multiple other suspicious activities seen in Prefetch (RUNDLL32 runs) and WEVTUTIL usage. This suggests the attacker had prior unauthorized access to this machine and installed F-Response on 2021-02-03, consistent with a long-dwell persistent attacker. (3) AppCompatCache (ShimCache) records subject_srv.exe with Modified=2018-04-10 — independently corroborating timestomping (the ShimCache recorded the backdated SI timestamp, not the true creation time). top_findings.description: Seven independent artifact sources confirm F-Response Subject Agent (subject_srv.exe) was deployed by an attacker from BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) to acquire the full disk image of base-wkstn-01 via raw kernel-level access, exfiltrating approximately 1.55 GB at 2021-09-16 03:07 UTC — constituting unauthorized full-disk exfiltration (T1005 + T1041) enabled by the F-Response BYOVD kernel driver (Mnemosyne.sys, T1014/T1068).
top_findings.alternative_hypothesis: subject_srv.exe is an authorized forensic imaging tool operated by the victim organization's own IT or security team conducting a legitimate disk acquisition of the workstation.
evidence_against_it: EVTX EID 4624 shows the authentication to base-wkstn-01 came from BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) using shieldbase\cbarton-a credentials via NTLM LogonType 3 — a lateral network logon, not a locally initiated authorized imaging session.

subject_srv.exe was timestomped to 2018-04-10 (USN BasicInfoChange|Close at 03:01:57 UTC confirms intentional $SI backdating) — authorized forensic tools are never timestomped as this would violate chain of custody.

Mnemosyne.sys kernel driver was installed and deleted within a 10-minute window (USN: drop at 02:52:10, delete at 03:01:03, reinstall at 03:01:59) — covert ephemeral driver pattern; authorized acquisitions maintain driver artifacts for the case record.
DKOM: conhost.exe PID 214668 was hidden from pslist via kernel linked-list unlinking (rootkit T1014) — legitimate forensic tools do not conceal companion processes.

top_findings.description: Three independent sources confirm attacker-controlled host BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) laterally accessed base-wkstn-01 using compromised domain credential shieldbase\cbarton-a via NTLM network logon, then immediately deployed F-Response as a service to perform the disk acquisition (T1550.002 / T1021.002): EVTX EID 4624 NTLM LogonType 3 burst from 172.16.5.25 at 02:51:50 UTC, memory network connection subject_srv.exe established to 172.16.5.25:5682 (F-Response controller port), and EID 7045 service install of 'F-Response Subject' at 03:01:57 UTC within 10 minutes of the logon burst.
top_findings.alternative_hypothesis: BASE-HUNT (172.16.5.25) is a legitimate IT administration workstation and the cbarton-a logon represents authorized remote administration of the workstation.
evidence_against_it: F-Response Subject Agent (a commercial disk acquisition tool) was installed as a Windows service immediately following the logon — authorized IT administration does not deploy raw disk imaging tools on workstations without documented change control.
Mnemosyne.sys (F-Response kernel driver) was loaded ephemerally and deleted within 10 minutes — covert operational security behavior incompatible with authorized administration.
DKOM rootkit technique was active during the session (conhost.exe PID 214668 hidden from pslist) — rootkit activity is not consistent with authorized IT work.
The logon used NTLM (not Kerberos) — NTLM is used when the attacker authenticates with a captured hash (Pass-the-Hash) or when the source machine is not domain-joined.

top_findings.description: Four independent artifact sources confirm the attacker timestomped subject_srv.exe to 2018-04-10 19:29:48 UTC at time of deployment (2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC) to evade timeline analysis and blend with legitimate binaries (T1070.006): MFT $SI<$FN divergence with uSecZeros=True and Copied=True flags, USN Journal BasicInfoChange|Close record at true creation time, ShimCache recording the backdated 2018-04-10 LastModifiedTimeUTC, and Registry AppCompatCache also preserving the backdated value.
top_findings.alternative_hypothesis: The 2018-04-10 timestamp reflects the legitimate compilation/packaging date of subject_srv.exe — an older binary version of F-Response that was installed from an archive without modification.
evidence_against_it: MFT $FN (the NTFS-kernel-maintained timestamp, not modifiable by user-mode APIs) shows EntryNumber 29211 was created on 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC — a 2018-compiled binary cannot have an MFT $FN creation time in 2021.

MFT uSecZeros=True flag: the microsecond fields of all four $SI timestamps are exactly zero — a statistical impossibility for a genuine file modification and the signature of timestomping tools that zero the sub-second component.

USN Journal (authoritative change log written by the NTFS kernel, cannot be forged) records an 0x800 (BasicInfoChange) reason code at close of the 2021-09-16 03:01:57 UTC write sequence — proving the $SI timestamps were changed at the moment the file was written, not pre-existing.
